title: Question 7
stem:
A stationary nucleus P of mass $243\text{u}$ decays by emitting an $\alpha$-particle of mass $4\text{u}$ to form a different nucleus Q, as illustrated in Fig. 7.1.

{{figure:figure_7_1}}

Fig. 7.1

The initial speed of the $\alpha$-particle is $1.6 \times 10^7 \text{m s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Use the principle of conservation of momentum to explain why the initial velocities of nucleus Q and the $\alpha$-particle must be in opposite directions.

markscheme_points.text: (total) momentum before (decay) is zero or P has zero momentum
(total momentum after decay must be zero so) α-particle and Q have momenta in opposite directions (and therefore velocities are in opposite directions)

hints: Hint 1: Think about the total momentum of nucleus P just before it breaks apart - what is its value if it is stationary?
Hint 2: If the total after must still equal that starting value, what must be true about the two momentum vectors when you add them together?
parts.proper_answer: Total momentum before decay is zero as P is stationary. Total momentum after must also be zero, so momenta of Q and alpha-particle must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, hence opposite velocities.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start from the stationary parent**
You have nucleus P sitting still before anything happens. Momentum is $p = mv$, so if $v = 0$, its momentum is zero. There are no external forces acting during the instant of decay, so total momentum is conserved.

Step 2: **Balance to zero after decay**
After decay you have two objects moving. Conservation gives: $$p_{total, before} = p_{total, after}$$ $$0 = p_Q + p_{\alpha}$$ This can only work if $p_Q = -p_{\alpha}$. The minus sign means opposite directions. Since masses are positive, the velocity vectors must also point in opposite directions.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Determine the initial speed $v$ of nucleus Q.
hints: Hint 1: First find the mass left for nucleus Q after the 4u alpha-particle has been removed from the 243u parent.
Hint 2: Set the magnitude of momentum of Q equal to the magnitude of momentum of the alpha-particle and rearrange for $v$ before substituting numbers.
parts.proper_answer: Mass of Q $= 243 - 4 = 239\text{ u}$. By conservation, $239v = 4 \times 1.6 \times 10^7$, giving $v = 2.7 \times 10^5\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the recoil mass**
Nucleon number is conserved in alpha decay. The parent is $243\text{ u}$ and the alpha is $4\text{ u}$, so what is left is: $$m_Q = 243\text{ u} - 4\text{ u} = 239\text{ u}$$ You can leave masses in u because the u will cancel on both sides.

Step 2: **Equate magnitudes of momentum**
Magnitudes must be equal for the total to cancel to zero: $$m_Q v = m_{\alpha} v_{\alpha}$$ $$239 \times v = 4 \times 1.6 \times 10^7$$ Solving: $$v = \frac{4 \times 1.6 \times 10^7}{239} = 2.7 \times 10^5\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ The recoil is much slower because Q is much heavier.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Calculate the initial kinetic energy, in MeV, of the $\alpha$-particle.
hints: Hint 1: Recall which kinetic energy expression links the given mass and speed of the alpha-particle, and what SI mass unit you must use.
Hint 2: Convert the 4u mass to kg using $1\text{ u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$ and calculate the energy in joules.
Hint 3: Think how to change a very small joule value into MeV using the $1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$ per eV relationship.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write kinetic energy in SI units**
For the alpha-particle: $$E_K = \frac{1}{2}m v^2$$ Mass must be in kg. One unified atomic mass unit $1\text{ u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, so: $$m = 4 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$$ and $v = 1.6 \times 10^7\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Calculate in joules**
Substitute: $$E_K = \frac{1}{2} \times (4 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}) \times (1.6 \times 10^7)^2$$ $$E_K = 8.5 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$$ This is tiny in joules, which is why nuclear energies use eV.

Step 3: **Convert J to MeV**
$1\text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$, so $1\text{ MeV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$. Divide: $$E_K = \frac{8.5 \times 10^{-13}}{1.60 \times 10^{-13}} = 5.3\text{ MeV}$$ Keep 2 significant figures to match the data.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A graph of number of neutrons $N$ against proton number $Z$ is shown in Fig. 7.2.

{{figure:figure_7_2}}

Fig. 7.2

The graph shows a cross that represents nucleus P.

A nucleus R has a nucleon number of 242 and is an isotope of nucleus P.

Nucleus R decays by emitting a $\beta^-$ particle to form a different nucleus S.
parts.text:
On Fig. 7.2, draw a cross to represent:

1. nucleus R (label this cross R)

2. nucleus S (label this cross S).
hints: Hint 1: Read Z and N for P from Fig. 7.2, then use the meaning of isotope to decide what stays the same and what changes for R with nucleon number 242.
Hint 2: Recall what happens to proton number and neutron number when a neutron changes to a proton in beta-minus decay to locate S from R.
parts.proper_answer: P is at $Z=95$, $N=148$. R is an isotope of P with $A=242$, so $Z=95$, $N=147$. S after beta-minus has $Z=96$, $N=146$. Plot R at (95,147) and S at (96,146).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Locate R from isotope idea**
From Fig. 7.2, P is at $Z = 95$, $N = 148$, so $A = Z+N = 243$ as expected. Isotope means same proton number, different neutrons. So R also has $Z = 95$. Its nucleon number is 242, so: $$N_R = A_R - Z = 242 - 95 = 147$$ That is one square straight down from P.

Step 2: **Locate S from beta-minus rules**
In $\beta^-$ decay a neutron becomes a proton: $$Z \rightarrow Z+1, \quad N \rightarrow N-1, \quad A \text{ unchanged}$$ So from R: $$Z_S = 95+1 = 96, \quad N_S = 147-1 = 146$$ That is one step right and one step down from R. Label the two crosses R and S clearly.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.text: State the name of the other lepton, in addition to the $\beta^-$ particle, that is emitted during the decay of nucleus R.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the beta-minus decay equation $n \rightarrow p + e^- + ?$ - what second light particle is needed to conserve energy and lepton number?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the full beta-minus equation**
A $\beta^-$ particle is an electron created when a neutron changes. To keep lepton number balanced and carry away extra energy, another lepton is emitted: $$n \rightarrow p + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e$$ That second particle is the electron antineutrino.
